opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most useful analogies for thinking about AI control, and it's often misunderstood.

The naive picture people have of a big tech company is that a software engineer at Google can SSH into a production machine and do whatever they want. That's not how it works at all. Google has tens of thousands of engineers, and they know that some small fraction of those people, at any given time, might be compromised. They might have been bribed, coerced by a foreign government, or they might just be disgruntled. So the security team has spent a huge amount of effort designing the system so that no individual engineer needs, or has, broad unilateral power over production systems or user data.

The basic move is this. Instead of giving people a general-purpose shell on the machine, you figure out the specific things engineers actually need to do. Restart this service, roll out this binary, look at these logs, change this config. Then you build narrow administrative APIs for exactly those actions. Each of those APIs can be designed so it's safe, logged, rate-limited, and, where it matters, requires a second person to approve. Code changes need review before they ship. Access to sensitive user data needs a justification tied to a ticket, gets audited, and might trigger an alert. If you really need to do something the APIs don't support, there's a break-glass procedure, but that's loud. It gets logged and scrutinized afterward.

What I find really important is the underlying philosophy. Google isn't trying to make it impossible for any engineer to ever do anything bad. That would make the company unable to function. They're trying to make the common, productive actions cheap and safe, and make the dangerous actions either impossible through normal channels or expensive and highly visible. The attacker has to do something weird, and weird things get noticed.

This is basically the frame I want people to bring to deploying powerful AI agents inside AI companies. Suppose you have a very capable model doing a lot of your research engineering, and you're not confident it's aligned. The question isn't "how do we make sure this thing is perfectly trustworthy?" It's "how do we structure its affordances so that even if it's scheming, it can't easily do something catastrophic, like exfiltrating its own weights or sabotaging the security infrastructure, without getting caught?" Many of the same tools apply. You give it narrow, permissioned interfaces instead of root access. You log everything. You have other models, or humans, review high-stakes actions. You make the dangerous actions require multiple independent parties to cooperate.

There are some interesting disanalogies, though. On one hand, AIs are in some ways easier to control than human insiders. You can monitor every single action they take, which you'd never do to your human employees. You can rerun them, test them in fake scenarios to see if they misbehave, and so on. On the other hand, the AIs might be doing a much larger share of the work, they might be smarter than the people reviewing them, and crucially, all the copies of the model might share the same misaligned goals. With human insiders, you're relying on the fact that it's unlikely that both the engineer and their code reviewer are compromised at once. If your reviewer is another instance of the same model, that assumption breaks, and you have to think carefully about collusion.

But overall, I think the Google example is encouraging. It shows that large organizations can get a lot of real work done while being robust to a meaningful fraction of their workforce being adversarial. That's an existence proof that the kind of thing we want for AI control isn't crazy.

r001.rationale: The response says engineers do not get a general-purpose shell and instead use narrow administrative APIs for predefined tasks such as restarting services, deploying binaries, and changing configuration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really interesting, and I think it's underappreciated how much of a model it is for what we might want to do with AIs.

So the basic situation at Google — and this is mostly from public writeups and talking to people who've worked there — is that Google has an enormous number of software engineers, and any individual one of them could in principle do a lot of damage. They could exfiltrate user data, they could insert a backdoor, they could delete production infrastructure. And Google can't just rely on having hired trustworthy people, because at that scale some fraction of your employees are going to be compromised, or coerced, or just disgruntled. So they've built their internal systems on the assumption that any given engineer might be an insider threat.

The way this cashes out is that engineers mostly don't have direct access to the things that matter. You don't SSH into a production machine and poke around. You interact with production through these administrative APIs, and the APIs are designed so that the dangerous actions are either impossible to do unilaterally or get logged and reviewed. So if you want to access user data for debugging, you go through a system that requires you to state a justification, maybe requires a second person to approve it, and the access is logged in a way that gets audited. If you want to push code, it has to go through code review, and the review tooling is set up so you can't easily sneak something past the reviewer. If you want to do something really drastic to infrastructure, it might require multi-party authorization — two people have to sign off at the same time.

And the thing that I think is really clever about this is that it's not primarily about catching bad actors after the fact. It's about structuring the affordances so that the bad action is hard to take in the first place, and so that taking it leaves evidence. Most of the security comes from the fact that the engineer only ever touches a narrow, well-defined interface rather than the underlying system.

The reason I care about this is that it's basically the situation we're going to be in with AI systems that we're using to do software engineering and AI research, but where we're not confident they're aligned. You've got an untrusted agent that's doing a lot of useful work, that needs some amount of access to be useful, and that might be trying to do something bad. And the Google approach suggests you don't have to solve the problem of making the agent trustworthy. You can instead design the environment so that an untrusted agent can't do that much damage — restrict what actions are available, make the risky ones require approval from something you trust more, log everything, and audit.

There are some important disanalogies, though. Google's insider threat model mostly assumes individual malicious insiders, or small numbers of them, who don't coordinate. If you're deploying many copies of the same AI model, and that model is misaligned, then all your "employees" are colluding by default. That breaks a lot of the assumptions behind multi-party authorization — two-person sign-off doesn't help if both people are the same scheming model. So in the AI case you need the approvers to be either humans or a more trusted, weaker model, and that's a big part of what the AI control agenda is about.

Another disanalogy is that Google's engineers are slow. A human can only take so many actions per day, so logging and auditing a sample of their actions is feasible. AI agents might take millions of actions, and you can't have a human look at all of them, so you need to be much more careful about what you review and how you use cheaper, weaker monitors to flag the suspicious stuff.

But overall, I think the Google case is really encouraging, because it's an existence proof that a large organization can get lots of useful work out of people it doesn't fully trust, by investing in infrastructure rather than by just hoping everyone is honest. And it's a fairly cheap thing to do — this stuff costs Google some engineering productivity, but not that much. I'd love for AI labs to take the same attitude toward their models that Google takes toward its engineers.

r001.rationale: The response says engineers generally lack direct access to production machines and instead use administrative APIs, so their actions are limited to a narrow, well-defined interface.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that the basic idea is to avoid giving engineers unrestricted access to production systems just because they need to do some administrative task. Instead, you expose particular operations through an administrative API. So you can restart a service, for example, without necessarily being able to read all the user data that service has access to.

That gives you a place to enforce permissions, log what people do, and require additional approval for particularly sensitive operations. The security benefit is that compromising an engineer’s account—or having an engineer who’s malicious—doesn’t automatically give you arbitrary control over everything they work on.

I don’t know the details of Google’s implementation well enough to vouch for exactly where those boundaries are. But that’s how I understand the general approach: make the access people need for their jobs narrower than the access that would let them cause a lot of damage.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes routing engineers’ administrative work through specific API operations, such as restarting a service, to avoid unrestricted access to production systems. It presents this as its understanding of Google’s approach, while qualifying that it cannot verify implementation details.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that Google tries to avoid giving engineers unrestricted access to production systems just because they work on them. Instead, you do a lot of administrative work through APIs that expose particular operations. You might be allowed to restart a service, for example, without being allowed to read all the user data that service handles.

That gives you a place to enforce permissions, require approval for especially sensitive actions, and log what happened. The idea is to let people do the work they need to do while limiting what a malicious engineer—or someone who compromises their account—can do.

I don’t know the details of Google’s internal setup well enough to say exactly where those boundaries are. But the general security principle is that access to maintain a system shouldn’t automatically mean access to everything in it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says engineers do administrative work through APIs exposing particular operations, such as restarting a service, rather than having unrestricted access to production systems.
